strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: The paper provides an insightful analysis of the 'fidelity–stability dilemma' in reconstruction-based MUAD methods (Section 2 and Appendix C), showing that decoders trained to invert information bottlenecks inevitably face high local Jacobian gains on benign variations.

Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks: RAD demonstrates superior performance over competitive training-based methods (e.g., Dinomaly, MambaAD, DiAD) across MVTec-AD, VisA, and Real-IAD, achieving particularly large gains in pixel localization metrics (e.g., +10.9 P-AP and +7.1 P-F1 on Real-IAD).

Thorough experimental evaluation: The evaluation covers standard MUAD, few-shot settings, data scaling/cold-start regimes, incremental class addition, multiple ViT foundation encoders, and detailed component ablations.

Practicality and adaptability: As an entirely training-free approach, RAD avoids costly multi-class training and catastrophic forgetting, allowing new samples or classes to be onboarded simply by appending features to the memory bank.
weaknesses: Backbone consistency in baseline comparisons: RAD defaults to a frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 encoder, whereas several compared baselines in Table 1 were originally trained and evaluated with different encoders (e.g., DINOv2 in Dinomaly, older backbones in UniAD/SimpleNet). While Appendix Table A2 validates RAD across backbones, a strictly controlled comparison holding the backbone fixed across baselines would make the empirical claims even more convincing.

Methodological novelty is evolutionary: The core algorithmic components—global image retrieval followed by locally constrained patch matching using multi-layer features—heavily draw upon concepts established in prior memory-based anomaly detection literature (e.g., SPADE, PatchCore, PNI).

Lack of detailed computational and memory profiling: While the limitations briefly note memory and latency overheads, the paper lacks concrete wall-clock inference times, FLOPs, and GPU RAM usage metrics compared to feed-forward reconstruction architectures, which is especially pertinent for large-scale benchmarks like Real-IAD.

Theoretical scope is basic: The theoretical justification in Section 4 rests on fundamental properties of distance-to-set functions (non-negativity, 1-Lipschitz continuity via the triangle inequality). While clean, it does not constitute a statistical generalization bound on anomaly detection performance.

strengths: Compelling and timely core thesis: The paper challenges the prevailing convention in multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection (MUAD) that task-specific decoder training or complex generative models are required, demonstrating that a well-designed training-free retrieval framework can surpass heavily trained models.

Strong and consistent empirical performance: RAD establishes new state-of-the-art results across standard benchmarks (MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, 3D-ADAM), achieving substantial gains in pixel-level localization metrics (e.g., +10.9 P-AP on Real-IAD, +6.3 P-AP on MVTec-AD). It also excels in the few-shot regime and under progressive data cold-start settings.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: The paper includes extensive evaluations across various foundation encoders (contrastive, MIM, supervised), resolution scaling, component ablations, and per-class breakdowns, clearly identifying the factors that drive performance.

Solid conceptual framing: The analysis of the fidelity–stability dilemma provides an intuitive and mathematically grounded rationale for why information-losing bottlenecks in autoencoder-like setups induce high decoder gain, and why non-expansive metric retrieval avoids this instability.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The algorithmic components (global image retrieval via CLS token followed by spatially-constrained nearest neighbor search across multi-scale patch embeddings) are heavily inspired by classic nearest-neighbor AD approaches (such as SPADE and PatchCore). The paper modernizes and combines these elements effectively for MUAD, but the algorithmic mechanisms themselves are standard.

Overstated theoretical claims: The assertion that retrieval 'provably upper-bounds' reconstruction residuals relies on assuming the reconstruction residual is a non-negative 1-Lipschitz function that vanishes on normal samples (Proposition D.2). In practice, trained neural decoders are generally not exactly 1-Lipschitz, making this formal connection more an idealized analogy than a literal bounding of practical encoder–decoder models.

Lack of detailed runtime and memory footprint profiling: Memory-based retrieval methods inherently trade training time for inference compute and storage overhead. While top-K filtering mitigates some inference costs, quantitative measurements of memory consumption (RAM/VRAM) and per-image inference latency across large datasets (e.g., Real-IAD with over 150k samples) are missing from the main evaluation.

strengths: The paper provides an insightful theoretical and conceptual critique of the ubiquitous encoder-decoder paradigm in multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection (MUAD), formalizing the fidelity-stability dilemma via Jacobian analysis of the bottleneck-decoder map.

RAD is entirely training-free, eliminating expensive task-specific decoder or diffusion training, yet consistently outperforms recent complex state-of-the-art training-based methods (e.g., Dinomaly, OmiAD, MambaAD) across multiple standard benchmarks (MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, 3D-ADAM).

Extensive empirical evaluations across diverse regimes: standard MUAD, few-shot MUAD, cold-start / incremental class scaling, foundation encoder comparisons, and thorough ablation studies validating the multi-layer memory, global context retrieval, and spatial conditioning.

The multi-level retrieval design effectively resolves the computational and semantic mismatch challenges of memory-based methods in multi-class settings by cascading global CLS-token retrieval with spatially constrained multi-layer patch matching.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental over established nearest-neighbor / memory-bank architectures: the core mechanism closely resembles combinations of SPADE and PatchCore adapted to Vision Transformers with global CLS filtering and local neighborhood constraints.

The theoretical contributions (Lemma 2.2, Lemma 4.1, Propositions D.1-D.2) largely formalize elementary geometric and Lipschitz properties of distance-to-set functions and linear operators; framing retrieval scores as theoretically 'upper-bounding' reconstruction residual performance is somewhat overstated.

The primary results in Table 1 rely on the recently proposed DINOv3 backbone, whereas several competing baselines were originally evaluated with weaker feature extractors. While Table A2 provides cross-encoder comparisons, the paper lacks a fully controlled re-evaluation of key baselines (e.g., Dinomaly) directly with DINOv3 under identical input resolutions.

The paper lacks quantitative evaluation of inference latency, FLOPs, and physical memory footprint. Storing multi-layer patch embeddings for large-scale datasets like Real-IAD is resource-intensive, and runtime comparisons against feed-forward reconstruction decoders are needed.

Key hyperparameters such as the number of retrieved reference images K (varying from 48 to 900) and neighborhood radius rho (ranging from 0 to 2) are tuned per dataset, leaving the sensitivity and automated selection of these parameters insufficiently explored.

strengths: The paper delivers a thought-provoking challenge to the dominant paradigm in multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection (MUAD), showing that a task-specific training-free retrieval framework can consistently outperform complex parametric encoder-decoder, diffusion, and distillation models.

The theoretical characterization of the fidelity–stability dilemma in reconstruction-based anomaly detection (Lemma 2.2) and the corresponding formal properties of retrieval-based scoring (non-expansiveness, empirical saturation, and near-optimal separation in Sec. 4 and App. D) provide clear intuition and mathematical grounding.

Extensive empirical validation across four diverse benchmarks (MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM) demonstrates substantial improvements, particularly on pixel-level localization metrics (e.g., +10.9 P-AP and +2.2 P-AUPRO on Real-IAD over Dinomaly).

Thorough experimental setups addressing realistic scenarios, including multi-class few-shot anomaly detection, incremental class onboarding, cold-start data scaling, controlled same-backbone comparisons (App. Tab. A6), and memory coreset compression.
weaknesses: The algorithmic formulation is conceptually an extension of classical memory-based nearest-neighbor methods (such as SPADE and PatchCore), combining [CLS]-based global image filtering with spatially constrained multi-layer patch retrieval. While effective, the algorithmic primitives themselves are relatively conventional.

The approach incurs substantial memory overhead when storing uncompressed multi-layer patch representations across large datasets (e.g., 60.8 GB on Real-IAD). Although coreset compression is tested on MVTec-AD in Table 3, a more systematic benchmark of memory compression across the larger Real-IAD dataset in the main paper would better demonstrate scalability.

The framework relies heavily on features from top-performing foundation models like DINOv3; as shown in Table A2, performance degrades notably with weaker or differently pre-trained backbones (e.g., BEiT, MAE), indicating strong sensitivity to the underlying representation quality.

Hyperparameters such as the global candidate size $K$ (ranging from 48 to 900) and neighborhood radius $ho$ (ranging from 0 to 2) vary across benchmarks, and the paper provides limited guidance on how practitioners should choose these parameters a priori on unseen domains without validation data.

strengths: Compelling paradigm shift: The paper convincingly challenges the prevailing consensus in multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection (MUAD) that task-specific decoder training is necessary, demonstrating that a training-free retrieval approach can outperform complex trained architectures.

Extensive and high-quality empirical evaluation: The authors conduct rigorous experiments across four standard and diverse benchmarks (MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM). RAD achieves state-of-the-art results, with especially substantial gains in pixel-level localization metrics (e.g., +10.9 P-AP and +7.1 P-F1 on Real-IAD).

Comprehensive scaling and ablation analysis: The submission thoroughly explores critical deployment dimensions, including cold-start and few-shot regimes (1- to 16-shot), incremental class additions, foundation encoder sweeps (evaluating 10 distinct ViT models), input resolutions, and hyperparameter sensitivity.

Effective and practical system design: The multi-level retrieval design—combining global context filtering via CLS tokens with spatially conditioned local neighborhood patch retrieval—elegantly circumvents cross-class contamination and reduces computational complexity from O(NP^2) to O(N + KP^2). Furthermore, coreset sampling demonstrates that memory can be compressed by ~98% with minimal performance degradation.

Principled conceptual motivation: The formulation of the fidelity–stability dilemma in reconstruction-based methods provides valuable insight into why bottlenecked encoder-decoder architectures either over-smooth defects or amplify benign noise, contrasting this with the non-expansiveness (1-Lipschitz stability) of retrieval scoring.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: The core building blocks—patch-level nearest-neighbor matching, multi-layer feature fusion, and spatial neighborhood priors—are conceptually similar to established single-class anomaly detection frameworks (e.g., PatchCore, SPADE, PNI). The primary technical novelty lies in the hierarchical combination with global CLS retrieval to scale to the multi-class setting.

Heavy reliance on strong self-supervised foundation backbones: RAD's high performance is closely coupled to representations from advanced self-supervised models such as DINOv3 and DINOv2. While the authors include a controlled same-backbone comparison against Dinomaly in Appendix I, the comparative table in the main text (Table 1) compares RAD against earlier baselines that used substantially weaker pre-trained feature extractors.

Inference latency and memory footprint: While coreset compression mitigates storage demands, storing multi-layer patch representations still imposes non-trivial memory overhead on large benchmarks (e.g., 60.8 GB uncompressed on Real-IAD). In addition, k-NN retrieval adds latency (44.7 ms/image on a high-end RTX 5090) compared to pure single-pass feed-forward architectures.

strengths: Compelling central message and timely question: The paper critically re-examines the prevailing dogma in multi-class unsupervised anomaly detection (MUAD) that task-specific decoder training or generative modeling is indispensable, demonstrating that a properly regularized retrieval framework can outperform complex learned models.

Insightful conceptual and theoretical framing: The identification and mathematical formalization of the fidelity–stability dilemma in reconstruction-based anomaly detection (Lemma 2.2) provides clear theoretical justification for why autoencoder-like architectures struggle with sensitivity and generalization, complemented by the non-expansiveness analysis of retrieval.

Well-motivated and effective system design: The proposed RAD framework cleanly addresses the key failure modes of naive nearest-neighbor search in MUAD via a hierarchical retrieval pipeline—global [CLS] retrieval to eliminate cross-category interference, local spatial neighborhood constraints to preserve structural layout, and multi-layer feature aggregation to combine fine-grained texture with semantic context.

Extensive and rigorous experimental validation: The authors evaluate RAD across four diverse benchmarks (MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM) across standard, few-shot, and cold-start/incremental settings. The supplementary material provides thorough ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, per-class tables, and same-backbone comparisons (Table A6) that confirm gains stem from the retrieval mechanism rather than solely from encoder strength.
weaknesses: Algorithmic component novelty is somewhat incremental: While the combination is well-tuned and effective for MUAD, the core algorithmic building blocks (memory banks, multi-layer ViT features, local neighborhood searching, and global image matching) are adaptations of well-known ideas from literature such as PatchCore, SPADE, and feature retrieval.

Memory storage and retrieval latency: Retaining uncompressed multi-layer patch representations requires significant storage (e.g., 60.8 GB on Real-IAD, 32.6 GB on MVTec-AD) and introduces non-trivial inference latency. Although Table 3 demonstrates the promise of coreset compression on MVTec-AD, a broader evaluation of coreset performance across more complex, multi-view benchmarks like Real-IAD in the main text would strengthen practical applicability.

Heavy reliance on specific foundation model pre-training objectives: As shown in Table A2, RAD's performance is tightly coupled to DINO-style contrastive/self-distillation representations (DINOv2/v3), whereas MIM-trained models (MAE, BEiT) perform substantially worse. The claim of being 'training-free' warrants the nuance that massive foundation-model pre-training is fundamentally required.
